      "path": "README.md",
      "content": "# dsh-folderwatch

**Wake the agent when the filesystem changes — not when you remember to look.**

An agent can already be woken on a clock (scheduled tasks) and on an HTTP request (webhooks). Neither covers the case that actually matters mid-session: something *outside* the conversation touches a file. A build finishes. A formatter rewrites the tree. A test runner drops a report. A download lands. A colleague pushes into a shared folder. Today the agent finds out only if it happens to look.

`dsh-folderwatch` arms a directory against the agent that armed it. When the tree changes, the agent receives an exact account of what changed — and can either be woken to act on it or simply find it waiting at its next step.

```
[folderwatch] 3 changes under /work/shop/reports
watch: reports · 14:02:11
1 created · 1 modified · 1 deleted
  + /work/shop/reports/run-42.json  18KB
  ~ /work/shop/reports/latest.json  18KB
  - /work/shop/reports/run-41.json
(4 events suppressed as this session's own writes)

Read the new report and summarise what failed.
```

## Why it is not just `fs.watch` and a callback

Three decisions separate a watcher you keep armed from one you uninstall after an afternoon:

### 1. Snapshots, not raw events

`fs.watch` reports that *something* happened, not *what*. It double-fires on Windows, sometimes reports no filename at all, and silently drops events under load. A watcher built directly on it tells the agent "something changed" — which is not enough to act on.

This plugin takes **snapshots and diffs them**. Renames, deletions and bursts are classified correctly on every platform, and each change arrives with its size. `fs.watch` is kept only as a *hint to rescan sooner*; the periodic rescan is the correctness path.

### 2. Echo suppression

A watcher on a directory the agent is editing has an obvious failure mode. The agent writes `src/app.ts`, the watcher fires, the agent is told `src/app.ts` changed, it reads the file it just wrote. That one settles — but a build, a formatter or a test runner the agent *itself* started keeps writing, and each write wakes the agent again. The result is a loop that burns tokens and reads as if the workspace were under attack by a stranger.

So tool calls that name a file are recorded in a short-lived ledger, and changes to those paths inside the window are counted as **suppressed** rather than delivered. The window is deliberately short (`echoWindowMs`, default 2500ms): a file the agent wrote ten minutes ago changing *now* is real news.

The suppression is visible rather than silent — every batch reports how many events it filtered, so you can tell "nothing happened" from "the agent did it itself".

### 3. Delivery is opt-in per watch

| mode | call | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `wake` *(default)* | `agent.followup(message)` | starts a new turn |
| `queue` | `agent.inject(message)` | waits for the agent's next step |

A watcher that can always interrupt is a watcher nobody leaves armed. The quieter option is one argument away, so you can arm a watch for a whole session without handing it the power to interrupt you.

## Install

```
dsh plugin add https://github.com/11111353535/dsh-folderwatch
```

From a checkout instead of a git host, pass the absolute path:

```
dsh plugin add /absolute/path/to/dsh-folderwatch
```

The package declares no `dsh-*` peer dependency on purpose: it imports only `node:*` plus `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools`, `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm` and `@deepseek-ai/schemastery`, all of which the harness resolves from its own installation. Nothing is bundled that could shadow the host's copy.

To tune it per profile, add a `config` block to the row the installer inserted in `~/.dsh/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: folderwatch
      name: 'dsh-folderwatch'
      config:
        quietMs: 400
        cooldownMs: 5000
        watches:
          - path: E:/work/reports
            label: reports
            pattern: '**/*.json'
            prompt: Read the new report and summarise what failed.
            mode: wake
```

| key | default | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `watches` | `[]` | Watches armed at load time. Arming from a session with the tool is the usual path. |
| `ignore` | build/VCS/dependency dirs | Ignore patterns applied to every watch, merged with each watch's own list. |
| `quietMs` | `400` | Quiet period before a batch is delivered. |
| `maxWaitMs` | `5000` | Ceiling on how long changes may wait for quiet, so a never-quiet tree still reports. |
| `cooldownMs` | `5000` | Minimum gap between deliveries for one watch. |
| `pollIntervalMs` | `1500` | How often the tree is rescanned. |
| `maxWatches` | `16` | Maximum number of simultaneously armed watches. |
| `maxEntries` | `20000` | Snapshot entry cap, guarding against a runaway tree. |
| `echoWindowMs` | `2500` | How long a path stays suppressed after this session writes it. |
| `maxEventsPerMessage` | `60` | Events listed in one notification before truncation. |

## Tools

### `folderwatch_add`

Arm a watch. Returns the arm report, or the reason it could not be armed.

| argument | type | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string *(required)* | Directory to watch. Absolute, or relative to the workspace. |
| `label` | string | Short name shown in listings and notifications. |
| `prompt` | string | Instruction appended to each notification, e.g. `re-run the failing test`. |
| `pattern` | string | Glob selecting which paths are reported, e.g. `**/*.log`. |
| `ignore` | string[] | Extra ignore patterns for this watch. A bare name like `tmp` matches at any depth. |
| `recursive` | boolean | Descend into subdirectories. Defaults to `true`. |
| `once` | boolean | Disarm after the first delivery. Defaults to `false`. |
| `mode` | `"wake"` \| `"queue"` | Delivery mode. Defaults to `wake`. |
| `sessionId` | string | Session to notify, when it is not the calling one. |

```
dsh-folderwatch · armed "reports"
  root:      /work/shop/reports
  watching:  12 file(s), 3 directories (recursive)
  pattern:   **/*.json
  ignoring:  node_modules, .git
  deliver:   wake the agent (followup)

Changes are reported in batches after the tree goes quiet, and this session's own writes are filtered out.
```

### `folderwatch_list`

The inventory: what each watch is watching, how often it has fired, and whether anything is pending.

```
dsh-folderwatch · 2 watches
  reports  running  12 file(s)  2 delivery(ies)  last fired 1m ago
    /work/shop/reports  [**/*.json]
  inbox  stopped  12 file(s)  0 delivery(ies)  never fired
    /work/shop/inbox
    3 change(s) pending delivery
```

### `folderwatch_check`

Rescan now and report what changed **without delivering a message**. This is how you answer "has anything happened yet" during a turn instead of waiting to be woken.

```
dsh-folderwatch · check "reports" · 3 change(s) since the last scan
  + /work/shop/reports/run-42.json  18KB
  ~ /work/shop/reports/latest.json  18KB
  - /work/shop/reports/run-41.json
  (4 further event(s) were this session's own writes)

This was a check: the snapshot advanced and no message was delivered.
```

### `folderwatch_fire`

Deliver a watch's pending changes immediately instead of waiting for the quiet period. Useful to confirm the delivery path works, or when a batch is known to be complete. When nothing is pending, it says so and sends nothing.

### `folderwatch_remove`

Disarm a watch and release its filesystem handles. Reports what it delivered while armed.

```
dsh-folderwatch · disarmed "reports"
  root: /work/shop/reports
  delivered 2 batch(es) over 7 event(s) while armed
  filtered 4 event(s) that were this session's own writes
```

## Slash command

```
/watch                                              # inventory
/watch add ./reports --pattern '**/*.json'          # arm, waking the agent
/watch add ./build --queue                          # arm, waiting for the next step
/watch add ./inbox --once                           # disarm after the first delivery
/watch check reports                                # rescan without delivering
/watch fire reports                                 # deliver now
/watch rm reports                                   # disarm
```

## Behaviour notes

- **Batching.** Changes are collected until the tree has been quiet for `quietMs`, or until `maxWaitMs` has passed, then delivered as one message. A `cooldownMs` gap prevents a churning tree from producing a stream of messages.
- **Recursive on Windows.** `fs.watch` with `recursive: true` is used where the platform supports it and falls back to a polled walk where it does not. The arm report names which path is in use (`watch+poll`, `poll`, …).
- **Snapshot caps.** A tree larger than `maxEntries` produces a partial snapshot; the arm report says so rather than silently under-reporting.
- **Unreadable directories** are counted and named (up to three) in the arm report instead of failing the watch.
- **Lifecycle.** Watches are registered as effects, so unloading the plugin closes every handle. A watch armed at load time from config still needs a live agent to deliver to; it resolves one by `sessionId` through the session controller.
- **Deletions.** A directory disappearing takes its children with it; the diff prunes nested deletions so a removed folder is one event, not one per file.

## Development

```
npm test           # 110 unit tests, no harness needed
npm run test:live  # four real watch scenarios against a temporary directory
npm run setup:deps
```

`lib/` is plain ESM JavaScript with no build step. The unit tests cover the pure modules — glob compilation, snapshot diffing, batching, echo extraction, and every renderer — and the live test covers what fixtures cannot: that a real `fs.watch` plus poll loop notices an external write, suppresses the session's own write, classifies a deletion, and applies a pattern filter.

```
dsh-folderwatch live check · win32
  ✓ delivered after an external write: external.txt
  ✓ suppressed this session's own write
  ✓ classified a deletion correctly
  ✓ applied the pattern filter
  4/4 scenarios passed
```

`setup:deps` links the host packages `lib/` imports (`cordis`, `dsh-tools`, `dsh-llm`, `schemastery`) into a local `node_modules` so a bare checkout can run the tests. Set `DSH_HOST_NODE_MODULES` if the harness is not in a standard location.

      "content": "/**
 * dsh-folderwatch — arm a directory and wake the agent when it changes.
 *
 * The harness can already wake an agent on a clock (scheduled tasks) and on an
 * HTTP request (webhooks). Neither covers the case that actually matters in a
 * working session: something outside the conversation touches a file. A build
 * finishes, a formatter rewrites the tree, a test runner drops a report, a
 * colleague pushes into a shared folder, a download lands. Today the agent finds
 * out only if it happens to look.
 *
 * This plugin closes that gap. A watch is armed against a directory and the
 * agent that armed it; when the tree changes — after the burst settles — the
 * agent receives a message describing exactly what changed, and can be woken to
 * act on it or simply have it waiting at its next step.
 *
 * Three design choices are worth stating up front, because they are the
 * difference between a watcher you keep and one you uninstall:
 *
 * 1. **Snapshots, not raw events.** `fs.watch` reports that something happened,
 *    not what; it double-fires on Windows and can miss changes under load. The
 *    watcher takes snapshots and diffs them, so renames, deletions and bursts
 *    are classified correctly on every platform. `fs.watch` is kept only as a
 *    hint to rescan sooner.
 * 2. **Echo suppression.** The agent's own writes must not wake the agent.
 *    Tool calls that name a file are recorded in a short-lived ledger, and
 *    changes to those paths inside the window are counted as suppressed rather
 *    than delivered. Without this, an agent editing a watched tree talks to
 *    itself in a loop.
 * 3. **Delivery is opt-in per watch.** `mode: 'wake'` calls `followup` and
 *    starts a turn; `mode: 'queue'` calls `inject` and waits for the agent's
 *    next step. A watcher that can always interrupt is a watcher nobody leaves
 *    armed, so the quieter option is one argument away.
 *
 * @module dsh-folderwatch
 */

import { existsSync, statSync } from 'node:fs'
import { resolve } from 'node:path'

import { createUserMessage } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm'
import { defineTool } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools'
import Schema from '@deepseek-ai/schemastery'

import { countEvents } from './diff.js'
import { createEchoLedger, pathsFromToolCall } from './echo.js'
import {
  renderArm,
  renderCheck,
  renderEvents,
  renderList,
  renderNotification,
  renderProblem,
  renderRemoval,
} from './format.js'
import { caseInsensitive, matchesAny, normalizePath, relativeTo, resolveWatchPath } from './match.js'
import { FolderWatch } from './watch.js'

/** Plugin name, as the profile's patch file refers to it. */
export const name = 'dsh-folderwatch'

/**
 * Services this plugin needs.
 *
 * A static array, not a function: the harness rejects a function form by
 * disabling the whole bundle, and a plugin that declares its services wrongly
 * fails silently rather than loudly. `sessionController` and `sessions` are
 * optional and reached through `ctx.get`, so a deployment without them loses
 * session-based delivery but keeps everything else.
 */
export const inject = ['tools', 'commands']

/** Directory names no watcher wants to hear about. */
const DEFAULT_IGNORE = [
  'node_modules',
  '.git',
  '.hg',
  '.svn',
  '.next',
  '.nuxt',
  '.cache',
  '.turbo',
  '.venv',
  'venv',
  '__pycache__',
  'dist',
  'build',
  'target',
  'coverage',
  '.DS_Store',
  'Thumbs.db',
]

/**
 * Per-profile configuration.
 *
 * Every knob that could reasonably differ between machines lives here rather
 * than in a constant, so tuning a profile never means editing code.
 */
export const Config = Schema.object({
  watches: Schema.array(
    Schema.object({
      path: Schema.string().description('Directory to watch, absolute or relative to the workspace.'),
      id: Schema.string().description('Optional stable id; derived from the path when omitted.'),
      label: Schema.string().description('Human-readable name shown in listings and notifications.'),
      prompt: Schema.string().description('Instruction appended to the notification the agent receives.'),
      pattern: Schema.string().description('Glob selecting which paths are reported, e.g. "**/*.ts".'),
      ignore: Schema.array(Schema.string()).description('Extra ignore patterns for this watch.'),
      recursive: Schema.boolean().description('Descend into subdirectories. Defaults to true.'),
      once: Schema.boolean().description('Disarm after the first delivery. Defaults to false.'),
      mode: Schema.string().description('"wake" starts a turn; "queue" waits for the next step.'),
      sessionId: Schema.string().description('Session to notify when the watch was not armed by a tool call.'),
    }),
  )
    .description('Watches armed at load time. Tool-armed watches are the usual path.')
    .default([]),
  ignore: Schema.array(Schema.string())
    .description('Ignore patterns applied to every watch, merged with the per-watch list.')
    .default(DEFAULT_IGNORE),
  quietMs: Schema.number().description('Quiet period before a batch is delivered.').default(400),
  maxWaitMs: Schema.number().description('Ceiling on how long changes may wait for quiet.').default(5000),
  cooldownMs: Schema.number().description('Minimum gap between deliveries for one watch.').default(5000),
  pollIntervalMs: Schema.number().description('How often the tree is rescanned.').default(1500),
  maxWatches: Schema.number().description('Maximum number of simultaneously armed watches.').default(16),
  maxEntries: Schema.number().description('Snapshot entry cap, guarding against a runaway tree.').default(20000),
  echoWindowMs: Schema.number().description('How long a path stays suppressed after this session writes it.').default(2500),
  maxEventsPerMessage: Schema.number().description('Events listed in one notification before truncation.').default(60),
})

/**
 * Turn a path into a stable, readable watch id.
 *
 * @param {string} root - absolute watch root.
 * @returns {string} id.
 */
function deriveId(root) {
  const tail = normalizePath(root).replace(/[:/]+/gu, '-').replace(/^-+|-+$/gu, '')
  const trimmed = tail.length > 48 ? tail.slice(tail.length - 48) : tail
  return trimmed === '' ? 'watch' : trimmed.toLowerCase()
}

/**
 * Resolve the workspace root for a tool call, when the harness can tell us.
 *
 * Optional service, optional answer: a deployment without a workspace registry
 * still watches absolute paths, it just cannot resolve relative ones against a
 * workspace.
 *
 * @param {import('@deepseek-ai/cordis').Context} ctx - plugin context.
 * @param {{ agent?: { session?: { id?: string } } }} exec - the tool execution.
 * @returns {string | undefined} absolute workspace root.
 */
function workspaceRootFor(ctx, exec) {
  try {
    const registry = typeof ctx.get === 'function' ? ctx.get('workspaceRegistry') : undefined
    if (registry === undefined) return undefined
    const session = exec?.agent?.session
    if (session !== undefined && typeof registry.forSession === 'function') {
      const root = registry.forSession(session)
      if (typeof root === 'string' && root !== '') return root
    }
    if (typeof registry.current === 'function') {
      const root = registry.current()
      if (typeof root === 'string' && root !== '') return root
    }
    if (typeof registry.defaultRoot === 'function') {
      const root = registry.defaultRoot()
      if (typeof root === 'string' && root !== '') return root
    }
  } catch {
    /* An optional service that misbehaves must not break the tool. */
  }
  return undefined
}

/**
 * Verify that a watch target exists and is a directory.
 *
 * Failing here, at arm time, with the actual path in the message is much better
 * than arming a watch that silently never fires because the path was a typo.
 *
 * @param {string} root - absolute path to check.
 * @returns {string | undefined} an error message, or undefined when usable.
 */
function checkTarget(root) {
  if (!existsSync(root)) return `no such path: ${root}`
  try {
    const info = statSync(root)
    if (info.isDirectory()) return undefined
    return `not a directory: ${root}`
  } catch (error) {
    return error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)
  }
}

/**
 * Build the plugin's live state.
 *
 * Kept in one closure so `apply()` reads as configuration rather than
 * bookkeeping, and so tests can construct it without a harness.
 *
 * @param {import('@deepseek-ai/cordis').Context} ctx - plugin context.
 * @param {object} config - validated configuration.
 * @returns {object} the registry and its helpers.
 */
function createRegistry(ctx, config) {
  /** @type {Map<string, FolderWatch>} */
  const watches = new Map()
  const echo = createEchoLedger({
    windowMs: config.echoWindowMs,
    caseInsensitive: caseInsensitive(),
  })
  let lastAgent

  /**
   * Remember the most recent agent seen, so a watch declared in configuration
   * (with no arming tool call) still has somewhere to deliver.
   *
   * @param {unknown} agent - candidate agent.
   * @returns {void}
   */
  function rememberAgent(agent) {
    if (agent !== undefined && agent !== null) lastAgent = agent
  }

  /**
   * Find a live agent to deliver to.
   *
   * Order: the agent that armed the watch, then the session it named, then the
   * most recent agent this plugin has seen. Each step is guarded — a session
   * that has since been archived must degrade to the next option, not throw.
   *
   * @param {FolderWatch} watch - the watch that fired.
   * @returns {Promise<object | undefined>} a live agent, when one can be found.
   */
  async function resolveAgent(watch) {
    if (watch.boundAgent !== undefined) {
      try {
        if (watch.boundAgent.session?.id !== undefined) return watch.boundAgent
      } catch {
        /* Disposed agents can throw on property access; fall through. */
      }
    }
    if (watch.sessionId !== undefined) {
      try {
        const controller = typeof ctx.get === 'function' ? ctx.get('sessionController') : undefined
        if (controller !== undefined && typeof controller.resolveAgent === 'function') {
          const found = await controller.resolveAgent(watch.sessionId)
          if (found?.agent !== undefined) return found.agent
        }
      } catch {
        /* Fall through to the session registry. */
      }
      try {
        const sessions = typeof ctx.get === 'function' ? ctx.get('sessions') : undefined
        const session = sessions?.get?.(watch.sessionId)
        if (session?.agent !== undefined) return session.agent
      } catch {
        /* Fall through to the last-seen agent. */
      }
    }
    return lastAgent
  }

  /**
   * Deliver one batch to the agent behind a watch.
   *
   * @param {{ diff: object, suppressed: number, truncated: boolean }} batch - the batch to deliver.
   * @param {FolderWatch} watch - the watch that fired.
   * @returns {Promise<void>} resolves after the message is handed over.
   */
  async function deliver(batch, watch) {
    const agent = await resolveAgent(watch)
    if (agent === undefined) {
      throw new Error('no live agent to notify; arm the watch from a session or set sessionId')
    }
    const text = renderNotification(
      { id: watch.id, root: watch.root, label: watch.label, prompt: watch.prompt },
      batch,
      { limit: config.maxEventsPerMessage, at: new Date().toISOString() },
    )
    const message = createUserMessage({
      content: [{ type: 'text', text }],
      source: { kind: 'folderwatch' },
    })
    if (watch.mode === 'queue' && typeof agent.inject === 'function') agent.inject(message)
    else if (typeof agent.followup === 'function') agent.followup(message)
    else if (typeof agent.inject === 'function') agent.inject(message)
    else throw new Error('the resolved agent exposes neither followup nor inject')
  }

  /**
   * Arm a new watch.
   *
   * @param {object} spec - watch specification.
   * @param {{ agent?: unknown, signal?: AbortSignal }} [origin] - the call that armed it.
   * @returns {Promise<{ ok: true, status: object } | { ok: false, error: string }>} the outcome.
   */
  async function arm(spec, origin = {}) {
    if (watches.size >= config.maxWatches) {
      return { ok: false, error: `too many watches armed (limit ${config.maxWatches}); remove one first` }
    }
    let root
    try {
      root = resolveWatchPath(spec.path, spec.workspace, resolve)
    } catch (error) {
      return { ok: false, error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error) }
    }
    const problem = checkTarget(root)
    if (problem !== undefined) return { ok: false, error: problem }

    const id = typeof spec.id === 'string' && spec.id !== '' ? spec.id : deriveId(root)
    if (watches.has(id)) return { ok: false, error: `a watch with id "${id}" is already armed` }

    const ignore = [...config.ignore, ...(Array.isArray(spec.ignore) ? spec.ignore : [])]
    const watch = new FolderWatch(
      {
        id,
        root,
        label: spec.label,
        pattern: spec.pattern,
        ignore,
        recursive: spec.recursive,
        once: spec.once,
        mode: spec.mode,
        prompt: spec.prompt,
        sessionId: spec.sessionId,
        quietMs: config.quietMs,
        maxWaitMs: config.maxWaitMs,
        cooldownMs: config.cooldownMs,
        pollIntervalMs: config.pollIntervalMs,
        maxEntries: config.maxEntries,
        echo,
      },
      deliver,
      (error) => {
        ctx.logger?.warn?.(`dsh-folderwatch: watch "${id}": ${error.message}`)
      },
    )
    if (origin.agent !== undefined) watch.boundAgent = origin.agent
    watches.set(id, watch)
    try {
      await watch.start(origin.signal)
    } catch (error) {
      watches.delete(id)
      return { ok: false, error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error) }
    }
    return { ok: true, status: watch.status() }
  }

  /**
   * Disarm a watch and release its handles.
   *
   * @param {string} id - watch id.
   * @returns {Promise<object | undefined>} the final status, when it existed.
   */
  async function disarm(id) {
    const watch = watches.get(id)
    if (watch === undefined) return undefined
    const status = watch.status()
    await watch.stop()
    watches.delete(id)
    return status
  }

  /**
   * Disarm everything; used when the plugin unloads.
   *
   * @returns {Promise<void>} resolves once every watch is stopped.
   */
  async function disarmAll() {
    for (const watch of watches.values()) await watch.stop()
    watches.clear()
  }

  return {
    watches,
    echo,
    arm,
    disarm,
    disarmAll,
    rememberAgent,
    resolveAgent,
    statuses: () => [...watches.values()].map((watch) => watch.status()),
    get: (id) => watches.get(id),
  }
}

/**
 * Register the tools, the command and the observation hooks.
 *
 * @param {import('@deepseek-ai/cordis').Context} ctx - plugin context.
 * @param {object} config - validated configuration.
 * @returns {void}
 */
export function apply(ctx, config) {
  const registry = createRegistry(ctx, config)

  /* Registered before the first await, as the plugin contract requires: an
   * await here would place the registrations outside the disposer window and
   * they would leak on unload. */
  ctx.effect(() => () => {
    void registry.disarmAll()
  })

  /**
   * Record the agent behind every tool result.
   *
   * Two jobs in one observer. It keeps `lastAgent` current, which is how a
   * configuration-declared watch finds somewhere to deliver; and it records the
   * paths this session wrote, which is what echo suppression reads. It is a
   * read-only observer of an immutable result, so it can never change what a
   * tool call returns.
   */
  ctx.on('tools/result', (exec) => {
    registry.rememberAgent(exec?.agent)
    if (typeof exec?.name !== 'string') return
    const { paths, certain } = pathsFromToolCall(exec.name, exec.arguments)
    if (paths.length === 0) return
    const absolute = paths.map((path) => resolveWatchPath(path, undefined, resolve))
    registry.echo.record(absolute, { certain })
  })

  ctx.tools.register(
    defineTool({
      name: 'folderwatch_add',
      description:
        'Watch a directory and wake this agent when its contents change. Use it when work depends on something outside the conversation that you cannot poll: a build output directory, a test report location, a shared hand-off folder, a download target. Changes are batched after the tree goes quiet, and this session\'s own writes are filtered out so the watch never reports the agent back to itself. Delivery defaults to waking the agent with a new turn; pass mode: "queue" to have the report wait until the agent\'s next step instead.',
      parameters: {
        path: { type: 'string', required: true, description: 'Directory to watch. Absolute, or relative to the workspace.' },
        label: { type: 'string', description: 'Short name for this watch, shown in listings and notifications.' },

import { resolve } from 'node:path'

const HINT_DEBOUNCE_MS = 120

/**
 * A live watch over one directory.
 *
 * Lifecycle is explicit: `start()` takes the first snapshot, `stop()` releases
 * every handle and timer. Nothing here touches the agent — delivery is a
 * callback the caller supplies, which keeps this class testable against a
 * temporary directory and free of any harness dependency.

   * @param {object} spec - the watch definition.
   * @param {string} spec.id - stable identifier.
   * @param {string} spec.root - absolute directory being watched.
   * @param {string[]} [spec.ignore] - ignore patterns.
   * @param {string} [spec.pattern] - glob selecting which paths count.
   * @param {boolean} [spec.recursive] - whether to descend.
   * @param {boolean} [spec.once] - disarm after the first delivery.
   * @param {number} [spec.quietMs] - quiet period before delivering.
   * @param {number} [spec.maxWaitMs] - ceiling on how long events may wait.
   * @param {number} [spec.cooldownMs] - minimum gap between deliveries.
   * @param {number} [spec.pollIntervalMs] - rescan interval.

   * @param {{ isEcho: (path: string) => boolean }} [spec.echo] - ledger of this session's own writes.
   * @param {(batch: object, watch: FolderWatch) => Promise<void>} onBatch - delivery callback.
   * @param {(error: Error, watch: FolderWatch) => void} [onError] - error sink.
   * @param {() => number} [now] - clock, injectable for tests.
   * @param {(path: string, options: object, listener: Function) => object} [watchFactory] - fs.watch, injectable for tests.

    this.root = normalizePath(spec.root)
    this.ignore = Array.isArray(spec.ignore) ? spec.ignore : []
    this.pattern = typeof spec.pattern === 'string' && spec.pattern !== '' ? spec.pattern : undefined
    this.recursive = spec.recursive !== false
    this.once = spec.once === true

    this.maxEntries = Number.isFinite(spec.maxEntries) ? spec.maxEntries : undefined

    this.label = typeof spec.label === 'string' && spec.label !== '' ? spec.label : undefined

    this.onBatch = onBatch
    this.onError = onError
    this.now = typeof now === 'function' ? now : () => Date.now()
    this.watchFactory = typeof watchFactory === 'function' ? watchFactory : fsWatch

    this.batcher = createBatcher({
      quietMs: Number.isFinite(spec.quietMs) ? spec.quietMs : 400,
      maxWaitMs: Number.isFinite(spec.maxWaitMs) ? spec.maxWaitMs : 5000,
      cooldownMs: Number.isFinite(spec.cooldownMs) ? spec.cooldownMs : 0,
    })

    this.deliveries = 0
    this.deliveredEvents = 0
    this.suppressedEvents = 0

   * says "4 events suppressed as your own writes" is evidence the filter is

      recursive: this.recursive,

   * @returns {void}
   */

  }

    } finally {

  /**

   * @param {{ created: object[], changed: object[], deleted: object[] }} diff - raw change set.

   */
  stage(diff) {

   *

   *

  async check() {

    const diff = diffSnapshots(this.snapshot, next.entries)
    const selected = applyWatchRules(diff, this)
    const { diff: filtered, suppressed } = this.suppressEchoes(selected)
    this.snapshot = next.entries
    this.truncatedSnapshot = next.truncated
    this.unreadable = next.unreadable
    return { diff: filtered, events: countEvents(filtered), suppressed }
  }

  /**
   * Deliver the pending batch through the caller's callback.
   *
   * @returns {Promise<void>} resolves after delivery.
   */
  async deliver() {
    const batch = this.batcher.drain()
    if (batch === undefined) return
    const events = countEvents(batch.diff)
    if (events === 0 && batch.suppressed === 0) return
    this.suppressedEvents += batch.suppressed
    try {
      await this.onBatch(batch, this)
      this.deliveries += 1
      this.deliveredEvents += events
      this.lastDeliveryAt = this.now()
      if (this.once) await this.stop()
    } catch (error) {
      this.report(error)
    }
  }

  /**
   * Note events dropped as echoes of the agent's own writes.
   *
   * @param {number} count - how many were dropped.
   * @returns {void}
   */
  noteSuppressed(count) {
    this.suppressedEvents += count
  }

  /**
   * Record an error without tearing the watch down.
   *
   * A watch that dies on the first transient filesystem error is worse than one
   * that reports the error and keeps trying.
   *
   * @param {unknown} error - the failure.
   * @returns {void}
   */
  report(error) {
    this.lastError = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)
    try {
      this.onError?.(error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(this.lastError), this)
    } catch {
      /* An error sink that throws must not become the error. */
    }
  }

  /**
   * Release every handle and timer.
   *
   * @returns {Promise<void>} resolves once stopped.
   */
  async stop() {
    if (this.state === 'stopped') return
    this.state = 'stopped'
    if (this.timer !== undefined) {
      clearInterval(this.timer)
      this.timer = undefined
    }
    if (this.hintTimer !== undefined) {
      clearTimeout(this.hintTimer)
      this.hintTimer = undefined
    }
    try {
      this.handle?.close?.()
    } catch {
      /* Already closed. */
    }
    this.handle = undefined
    this.batcher.reset()
  }

  /**
   * A serialisable view of the watch, for listing.
   *
   * @returns {object} status snapshot.
   */
  status() {

    return {
      id: this.id,
      root: this.root,
      label: this.label,
      pattern: this.pattern,
      ignore: this.ignore,
      recursive: this.recursive,
      once: this.once,
      mode: this.mode,
      prompt: this.prompt,
      sessionId: this.sessionId,
      state: this.state,
      watchKind: this.watchKind,
      files: counts.files,
      directories: counts.directories,
      pending: this.batcher.pending(),
      deliveries: this.deliveries,
      deliveredEvents: this.deliveredEvents,
      suppressedEvents: this.suppressedEvents,
      lastDeliveryAt: this.lastDeliveryAt === undefined ? undefined : new Date(this.lastDeliveryAt).toISOString(),
      lastError: this.lastError,
      truncatedSnapshot: this.truncatedSnapshot,
      unreadable: this.unreadable.slice(0, 20),
      createdAt: new Date(this.createdAt).toISOString(),
    }
  }
}

/**
 * Resolve a changed path into the relative form a watch reports.
 *
 * @param {FolderWatch} watch - the watch that owns the path.
 * @param {string} path - absolute path from a tool call.
 * @returns {string | undefined} relative path, or undefined when outside the root.
 */
export function relativizeFor(watch, path) {
  const relative = relativeTo(path, watch.root, { caseInsensitive: process.platform === 'win32' || process.platform === 'darwin' })
  return relative === null ? undefined : relative
}

      "path": "README.md",
      "content": "# dsh-reaper

**Reclaim the ports your agent forgot to give back.**

An agent starts `vite`, `next dev`, a watcher, a tunnel. The turn ends. The session ends. The process does not — it keeps holding 5173, and the next run dies with `EADDRINUSE` while you go hunting through Task Manager for a `node.exe` you cannot identify.

`dsh-reaper` inventories every listening endpoint on the machine, **attributes each holder to this session**, shows you exactly what it would kill, and only then — when you say `confirm: true` — reclaims the ports.

```
$ /reap

dsh-reaper · win32 · 2026-10-16T10:57:26.626Z
workspace: E:\work\shop-frontend

51 listening endpoint(s) · 432 process(es) · 3 reclaimable

 5173  tcp  agent-spawned  pid   8899   18m  node.exe
      node E:\work\shop-frontend\node_modules\.bin\vite --host
 3001  tcp  workspace      pid   9120   42m  node.exe
      node E:\work\shop-frontend\server.js
 3306  tcp  system         pid   9168  9h29m  mysqld.exe
      ↳ port 3306 is a well-known service port
19387  tcp  protected      pid  11664   2h9m  DeepSeek Harness.exe
      ↳ holds the harness process tree
```

## Why it is not just "kill by port"

Port tools tell you *what* holds a port. The hard part is deciding **whether you are allowed to kill it**, and that answer depends on facts a port number does not carry:

- Did this process descend from **the harness that is running the scan**? Killing it takes down the session.
- Is it **the machine's own infrastructure** — `mysqld` on 3306, `nginx` on 80?
- Is it a leftover **dev server** with no session tie at all?
- Is it something the user explicitly said to leave alone?

`dsh-reaper` answers that per endpoint and grades the result, so a `--all` sweep can be safe:

| verdict | meaning | auto-selected by `all: true` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `agent-spawned` | descends from the harness host process | ✅ |
| `workspace` | command line names the current workspace | ✅ |
| `dev-server` | looks like a dev server, watcher or tunnel | ❌ |
| `unattributed` | listening, but nothing ties it to this session | ❌ |
| `system` | OS process, or holds a well-known service port | ❌ |
| `protected` | matched `neverKill` / `protectPorts`, or holds the harness tree | ❌ |

Two rules make that table trustworthy:

1. **The harness never kills itself.** The scan walks up from its own pid and refuses the whole ancestor chain, plus the process tree it is running inside.
2. **Infrastructure is not "unattributed".** A holder of a well-known service port is graded `system` — the same hands-off grade as an OS process — so `all: true` never reaches it, and its note says `left alone` rather than hinting at an override.

## Safety properties

Reaping is destructive, so the defaults are conservative and the refusals are absolute:

- **Nothing is signalled without `confirm: true`.** The default call computes the plan and returns it.
- **The plan is the full descendant closure.** Killing an `npm run dev` shim without its child leaves the port held — the exact failure this plugin exists to prevent. Descendants are ordered deepest-first so children die before their parents.
- **Refusals cannot be overridden by naming a pid.** The harness process tree, pid 0–4, `neverKill` matches and `protectPorts` holders are refused even when passed explicitly, with the reason reported.
- **`SIGTERM` first, `SIGKILL` only if you ask.** `force: true` escalates, and even then survivors are reported rather than hidden.
- **The result is verified, not assumed.** After signalling, the plugin re-probes each freed port and reports `ports confirmed free` or `ports still held`.

## Install

```
dsh plugin add https://github.com/11111353535/dsh-reaper
```

From a checkout instead of a git host, pass the absolute path:

```
dsh plugin add /absolute/path/to/dsh-reaper
```

The package declares no `dsh-*` peer dependency on purpose: it imports only `node:*` plus `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools`, which the harness resolves from its own installation. Nothing is bundled that could shadow the host's copy.

To tune it per profile, add a `config` block to the row the installer inserted in `~/.dsh/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: reaper
      name: 'dsh-reaper'
      config:
        neverKill: ['my-precious-daemon']
        protectPorts: [80, 443, 19387]
        includeUdp: false
        graceMs: 3000
        scanTimeoutMs: 20000
```

| key | default | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `neverKill` | `[]` | Process-name or command-line substrings that must never be signalled. |
| `protectPorts` | `[]` | Ports whose holder is refused even when named explicitly. The harness's own web port is added automatically. |
| `includeUdp` | `false` | Also enumerate UDP endpoints. Off by default: dev servers are TCP. |
| `graceMs` | `3000` | How long `SIGTERM` gets before the process is reported as surviving. |
| `scanTimeoutMs` | `20000` | Wall-clock ceiling for one system enumeration. |

## Tools

### `reaper_scan`

Read-only inventory. Signals nothing. Grades every listening endpoint and returns the full scan.

| argument | type | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `includeUdp` | boolean | Also enumerate UDP endpoints. |
| `workspace` | string | Workspace root used for attribution. Defaults to the session workspace. |

### `reaper_reap`

Compute a plan and, only with `confirm: true`, execute it.

| argument | type | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pids` | integer[] | Explicit root pids. Their descendants are included automatically. |
| `ports` | integer[] | Reap whatever holds these ports. |
| `all` | boolean | Also select every endpoint confidently attributable to this session (`agent-spawned` and `workspace` only). |
| `force` | boolean | Escalate to `SIGKILL` for processes that ignore `SIGTERM`. |
| `confirm` | boolean | Actually signal the plan. Defaults to `false`. |

### `reaper_free_port`

Reclaim one specific port. If the port is already free it says so and does nothing; if the holder cannot be attributed or is protected, it reports why instead of guessing.

| argument | type | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `port` | integer *(required)* | The TCP port to reclaim. |
| `force` | boolean | Escalate to `SIGKILL` if `SIGTERM` is ignored. |
| `confirm` | boolean | Actually signal the holder. Defaults to `false`. |

## Slash command

```
/reap                  # inventory
/reap --all            # preview everything confidently attributable to this session
/reap --all --confirm  # and actually do it
/reap 5173             # preview reclaiming one port
/reap 5173 3001 --confirm --force
```

## How the scan works

| platform | endpoints | process table |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows | `Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen` (+ `Get-NetUDPEndpoint`) | `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` |
| Windows (fallback) | `netstat -ano` | `tasklist /FO CSV /NH` |
| Linux | `ss -H -ltnp` | `ps -eo pid=,ppid=,comm=,etimes=,args=` |
| macOS | `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -Fpcn` | `ps` |

Every probe is best-effort: a missing binary or a failed command degrades that one source and is reported in `degraded: ...` at the end of the scan. A scan that falls back to `netstat` still works — it just loses command lines, and therefore attribution gets weaker, which the report tells you.

One process listening on both `::` and `0.0.0.0` is one problem, not two: dual-stack bindings are collapsed into a single row per `protocol`/`port`/`pid`, with every address kept in `addresses`.

## Development

```
npm test          # 42 unit tests, no harness needed
npm run test:live # a real read-only scan of this machine
npm run setup:deps
```

`lib/` is plain ESM JavaScript with no build step, and the unit tests cover the parsers against recorded fixtures — Windows and BSD `netstat` tables, `ss`, `lsof`, `ps`, `tasklist`, the classifier, the plan builder, and the renderers. `test:live` covers what fixtures cannot: that the real enumeration works on the host you are on. It signals nothing.

`setup:deps` links the three host packages `lib/` imports (`cordis`, `dsh-tools`, `schemastery`) into a local `node_modules` so a bare checkout can run the tests. Set `DSH_HOST_NODE_MODULES` if the harness is not in a standard location.

      "path": "lib/index.js",
      "content": "/**
 * dsh-reaper — orphan process and port reaper for DeepSeek Harness.
 *
 * ## The problem this solves
 *
 * An agent starts a dev server, a watcher, or a tunnel to check its work, and
 * then the turn ends. The process does not. Twenty minutes later the next
 * `npm run dev` dies with `EADDRINUSE`, and the thing holding the port is a
 * node process whose only distinguishing feature is a command line the agent
 * itself wrote three turns ago and has since forgotten.
 *
 * Existing port tooling answers "what holds port 3000". That is the easy half
 * and it is already well served. The hard half is *attribution*: of the
 * forty-odd listening sockets on a working machine, which ones belong to this
 * harness, and of those, which ones will not come back if they are killed.
 * This plugin grades every listener on that question and refuses to touch
 * anything it cannot attribute.
 *
 * ## Design commitments
 *
 * - **Preview is the default.** `reaper_reap` signals nothing unless the
 *   caller passes `confirm: true`. The preview path computes the identical
 *   plan, so what you approve is what runs.
 * - **Refusals are hard.** The harness's own ancestor chain, pid 0-4,
 *   `neverKill` patterns and `protectPorts` are refused, and re-checked
 *   immediately before each individual signal.
 * - **Trees, not pids.** Killing a `npm run dev` shim without its child leaves
 *   the port held, which is the exact failure this plugin exists to fix. Plans
 *   always include the descendant closure, signalled deepest-first.
 * - **Optional services are consumed defensively.** `workspaceRegistry` is
 *   read through `ctx.get` and the plugin works without it, because a plugin
 *   that refuses to load when one seam is absent is worse than a plugin that
 *   degrades.
 *
 * ## Tools
 *
 * - `reaper_scan` — graded inventory of listening endpoints and their holders.
 * - `reaper_reap` — plan, preview, and (on `confirm: true`) terminate trees.
 * - `reaper_free_port` — reclaim one specific port, refusing to guess.
 * - `/reap` — the same inventory as a slash command, for a human at the UI.
 *
 * @module dsh-reaper
 */

import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises'

import { defineTool } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools'
import Schema from '@deepseek-ai/schemastery'

import { buildKillPlan, classify, isAutoSelectable, verdictRank } from './attribute.js'
import { renderPlan, renderScan } from './format.js'
import { terminate, waitForPortsReleased } from './kill.js'
import { probePorts } from './probe.js'
import { ancestorChain, scanSystem } from './scan.js'

export const name = 'dsh-reaper'

/** Services this plugin touches; every one is required for `apply` to run. */
export const inject = ['tools', 'commands']

/**
 * The pids that belong to the harness's own process tree: this process plus
 * everything it sits under.
 *
 * `ancestorChain` deliberately excludes its starting pid, so the caller joins
 * the two halves here. These pids are never reap candidates — killing one would
 * take down the harness that is running the scan.
 *
 * @param {Array<{ pid: number, ppid: number }>} processes - process table.
 * @returns {Set<number>} protected pids.
 */
function selfChainFor(processes) {
  const chain = new Set([process.pid])
  for (const pid of ancestorChain(processes, process.pid)) chain.add(pid)
  return chain
}

/**
 * Per-profile configuration. Every knob the plugin has lives here, so a
 * deployment can retune it from `cordis.patch.yml` without touching code.
 */
export const Config = Schema.object({
  /** Process-name or command-line substrings that must never be signalled. */
  neverKill: Schema.array(Schema.string()).default([]).description(
    'Process name or command-line substrings that dsh-reaper must never signal.',
  ),
  /** Ports whose holder is refused even when named explicitly. */
  protectPorts: Schema.array(Schema.number()).default([]).description(
    'Ports whose holders dsh-reaper must refuse to signal, even when named explicitly.',
  ),
  /** Whether the scan also enumerates UDP endpoints. */
  includeUdp: Schema.boolean().default(false).description(
    'Include UDP endpoints in the scan. Off by default: dev servers are TCP.',
  ),
  /** How long a graceful SIGTERM gets before a forced kill is offered. */
  graceMs: Schema.number().default(3000).description(
    'Milliseconds to wait for a process to exit after SIGTERM before reporting it as surviving.',
  ),
  /** Wall-clock ceiling for one system enumeration. */
  scanTimeoutMs: Schema.number().default(20_000).description(
    'Milliseconds allowed for one system enumeration before it is abandoned.',
  ),
})

/**
 * Pull the harness's own web port out of the environment so the plugin never
 * offers to reap the UI it is running inside.
 *
 * @param {string | undefined} webUrl - the `DSH_WEB_URL` value.
 * @returns {number[]} ports to protect by default.
 */
export function defaultProtectedPorts(webUrl) {
  if (typeof webUrl !== 'string' || webUrl === '') return []

    const session = exec?.agent?.session

    if (typeof registry.current === 'function') {

/**
 * Run one enumeration and grade every endpoint against the current session.
 *
 * @param {any} ctx - the plugin context.
 * @param {any} config - resolved plugin configuration.
 * @param {any} exec - the tool execution record.
 * @param {{ includeUdp?: boolean, workspace?: string }} [options]
 * @returns {Promise<any>} the graded scan.

async function runScan(ctx, config, exec, options = {}) {
  const includeUdp = options.includeUdp ?? config.includeUdp
  const raw = await scanSystem({
    includeUdp,
    timeoutMs: config.scanTimeoutMs,
    signal: exec?.signal,
  })

  const selfChain = selfChainFor(raw.processes)
  const protectPorts = [
    ...new Set([...config.protectPorts, ...defaultProtectedPorts(process.env.DSH_WEB_URL)]),
  ]
  const workspaceRoot = options.workspace ?? workspaceRootFor(ctx, exec)

  const graded = classify({
    listeners: raw.listeners,
    processes: raw.processes,
    hostPid: process.pid,
    selfChain,
    workspaceRoot,
    protectPorts,
    neverKill: config.neverKill,
  })

  const endpoints = graded.endpoints
    .map((row) => ({ ...row, rank: verdictRank(row.verdict) }))
    .sort((a, b) => a.rank - b.rank || a.port - b.port)

  const counts = {}
  for (const row of endpoints) counts[row.verdict] = (counts[row.verdict] ?? 0) + 1

  return {
    platform: raw.platform,
    scannedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    workspaceRoot,
    hostPid: process.pid,
    protectedPorts: protectPorts,
    endpoints,
    verdicts: counts,
    summary: {
      listeners: endpoints.length,
      processes: raw.processes.length,
      reapable: endpoints.filter((row) => isAutoSelectable(row.verdict)).length,
    },
    degraded: raw.degraded,
  }
}

/**
 * Select the root pids a reap call should act on.
 *
 * `all: true` selects only verdicts the classifier considers safe to select
 * automatically — never `system`, `unattributed` or `protected`. Explicit
 * `pids` bypass that filter but still pass through the hard refusal list when
 * the plan is built.
 *
 * @param {any} scan - a graded scan.
 * @param {{ pids?: number[], ports?: number[], all?: boolean }} args - tool arguments.
 * @returns {{ roots: number[], notes: string[] }} selected roots and notes.

export function selectRoots(scan, args) {
  const notes = []
  const roots = new Set()

  for (const pid of args.pids ?? []) roots.add(pid)

  for (const port of args.ports ?? []) {
    const matches = scan.endpoints.filter((row) => row.port === port)
    if (matches.length === 0) {
      notes.push(`port ${port}: nothing is listening`)
      continue
    }
    for (const row of matches) {
      if (row.pid === null) {
        notes.push(`port ${port}: holder pid unknown, refusing`)
        continue
      }
      roots.add(row.pid)
    }
  }

  if (args.all === true) {
    const auto = scan.endpoints.filter((row) => isAutoSelectable(row.verdict))
    if (auto.length === 0) notes.push('no endpoint was confidently attributable to this session')
    for (const row of auto) {
      if (row.pid !== null) roots.add(row.pid)
    }
    for (const row of scan.endpoints) {
      if (isAutoSelectable(row.verdict) || row.pid === null) continue

       * "name it explicitly to include it" next to nginx is how a machine's own
       * daemon gets killed by an agent that was only trying to be helpful. */
      if (row.verdict === 'protected' || row.verdict === 'system') {

        continue
      }
      notes.push(`port ${row.port}: ${row.verdict} — not auto-selected (name it explicitly to include it)`)
    }
  }

  return { roots: [...roots].sort((a, b) => a - b), notes }

/**
 * Build the plan and, when confirmed, execute it.
 *
 * @param {any} ctx - the plugin context.
 * @param {any} config - resolved plugin configuration.
 * @param {any} exec - the tool execution record.
 * @param {any} args - tool arguments.
 * @returns {Promise<any>} plan plus optional outcome.
 */
async function reap(ctx, config, exec, args) {
  const scan = await runScan(ctx, config, exec, {})
  const { roots, notes } = selectRoots(scan, args)

  if (roots.length === 0) {
    return {
      confirmed: args.confirm === true,
      force: args.force === true,
      targets: [],
      refused: [],
      freedPorts: [],
      untouched: [],
      notes,
      scan,
    }
  }

  const processes = await loadProcesses(exec, config)
  const selfChain = selfChainFor(processes)
  const plan = buildKillPlan({
    processes,
    listeners: scan.endpoints,
    roots,
    selfChain,
    protectPorts: scan.protectedPorts,
    neverKill: config.neverKill,
  })

  if (args.confirm !== true) {
    return { ...plan, confirmed: false, force: args.force === true, notes, scan }
  }

  const ports = plan.freedPorts.map((row) => row.port)
  const outcome = await terminate({
    targets: plan.targets,
    force: args.force === true,
    graceMs: config.graceMs,
    signal: exec?.signal,
  })

  const release = ports.length > 0 ? await waitForPortsReleased(ports, { signal: exec?.signal }) : { released: [], stillHeld: [] }

  return {
    ...plan,
    confirmed: true,
    force: args.force === true,
    outcome,
    portsReleased: release.released,
    portsStillHeld: release.stillHeld,
    notes,
    scan,
  }
}

/**
 * Re-read the process table for plan building.
 *
 * Deliberately a second read rather than a cached one: the table the scan saw
 * may already be stale, and a plan built on a stale parent/child map can miss
 * a descendant or, worse, target a recycled pid.
 *
 * @param {any} exec - the tool execution record.
 * @param {any} config - resolved plugin configuration.
 * @returns {Promise<any[]>} the process table.
 */
async function loadProcesses(exec, config) {
  const raw = await scanSystem({ includeUdp: false, timeoutMs: config.scanTimeoutMs, signal: exec?.signal })
  return raw.processes
}

 *
 * @param {number} pid - target pid.
 * @param {NodeJS.Signals} signal - signal to send.
 * @returns {{ ok: boolean, reason?: string }} outcome.

    process.kill(pid, signal)
    return { ok: true }
  } catch (error) {
    const code = /** @type {NodeJS.ErrnoException} */ (error).code
    if (code === 'ESRCH') return { ok: false, reason: 'already exited' }
    if (code === 'EPERM') return { ok: false, reason: 'permission denied' }
    return { ok: false, reason: code ?? String(error) }
  }

      emit({ pid: target.pid, name: target.name, action: 'survived', detail: 'unresponsive to SIGKILL' })

    }
  }

      "path": "README.md",
      "content": "# dsh-which

**Command resolution forensics for DeepSeek Harness.** When you type `node`, a shell answers with a rule that is longer than people remember — PATH order, then PATHEXT on Windows or the executable bit elsewhere, with builtins short-circuiting the whole thing. `dsh-which` reports what that rule actually decided, what it shadowed, what shape PATH itself is in, and whether the copies behind one name agree on a version.

Every failure it names is silent. The command runs; it is just not the one you meant.

```
dsh-which · node
  winner:   C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.EXE
  kind:     native binary
  from:     PATH[0]  C:\Program Files\nodejs
  size:     84MB
  modified: 2025-11-03T09:14:00.000Z
  version:  v24.13.0  (--version)
  searched: 9 PATH entries

  shadowed — 1 other directory holds this name:
    PATH[6]  C:\Users\me\scoop\shims\node.EXE  native binary  84MB
      ↳ reports v20.11.1

  ⚠ the copies behind this name report different versions — the one that runs is the one at PATH[0].
```

That last block is the whole reason this exists. Two Node installations, one on PATH, and nothing anywhere tells you which one a command gets.

## Why not just run `which`

1. **`which` does not exist on Windows**, and where it does exist it answers a narrower question. It reports the file it found; it does not report the file it skipped.
2. **`which` inherits the rules under investigation.** Shelling out to a resolver to explain resolution means trusting the resolver you are debugging. The rules here are reimplemented as pure functions over an injected filesystem (`lib/resolve.js`), so they are testable against fixtures instead of against whatever is installed on the test machine.
3. **Shell builtins are not files.** `which cd` on most systems walks every PATH entry to report something that has nothing to do with what runs. This plugin says `builtin` and explains that PATH was never consulted.
4. **The interesting output is the shadowed copy.** "What runs" is one line. "What else answers to this name, and why is it not running" is the diagnosis — a stale global install behind a fresh local one, a `.cmd` shim in front of a real binary, a file that exists but was never made executable.
5. **Reporting is the whole job.** There is no PATH-editing tool here. A plugin that silently rewrites PATH is a plugin that breaks a machine.

## Install

```sh
dsh plugin add https://github.com/11111353535/dsh-which
```

From a checkout instead of a git host, pass the absolute path:

```sh
dsh plugin add /absolute/path/to/dsh-which
```

Optional configuration, in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- id: which
  name: 'dsh-which'
  config:
    probeByDefault: false        # run a version probe on every resolve
    probeShadowedByDefault: false # probe the shadowed copies too
    probeTimeoutMs: 4000
    maxSweepFiles: 400
    runtimes: [node, npm, pnpm, python, git]
```

| key | default | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `probeTimeoutMs` | `4000` | How long a version probe may take before it is abandoned. |
| `probeByDefault` | `false` | Probe every resolve without being asked. Slower, explains more. |
| `probeShadowedByDefault` | `false` | Probe the shadowed copies too. Multiplies the process spawns. |
| `maxSweepFiles` | `400` | Files examined in one sweep, so a huge directory cannot stall a session. |
| `runtimes` | node, npm, pnpm, yarn, bun, python, python3, pip, pip3, uv, git, rg, fd, make, pwsh, bash | Commands the environment report resolves. |

Probing is off by default because it spawns processes, and a diagnostic that costs four seconds on every call is a diagnostic people turn off.

## Tools

### `which_resolve`

Resolve one command and report what runs, what it shadowed, and — on request — what each copy reports as its version.

| parameter | type | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `command` | string, **required** | A name (`node`) or a path (`./build.sh`, `C:\tools\x.exe`). |
| `probe` | boolean | Run the winner with a version flag. |
| `probeShadowed` | boolean | Probe the shadowed copies too, so versions can be compared. |

A name that resolves to nothing is an answer, not an error:

```
dsh-which · build
  not found
  the name exists on PATH but nothing with that name is runnable
  searched: 45 PATH entries

  the name exists, but nothing with it can run:
        build  not runnable  1KB
        build  not runnable  1KB
        build  not runnable  1KB
        build  not runnable  1KB
        build  not runnable  1KB
        build  not runnable  1KB
        build  not runnable  1KB
        build  not runnable  1KB
        … and 37 more
```

The count is the finding; the enumeration is the evidence, and past eight directories the evidence stops being read. The lines that save an hour are the second and third: the name *is* on PATH, the file simply cannot run. On POSIX that means no executable bit — a shell walks right past it into later PATH entries, or fails.

An explicit path never consults PATH, and the report says so:

```
dsh-which · /repo/scripts/build.sh
  winner:   /repo/scripts/build.sh
  kind:     script
  from:     given as a path, PATH was not consulted
  size:     2.3KB
  searched: 0 PATH entries
```

### `which_path`

The shape of PATH itself: every entry in resolution order, with duplicates, entries whose directory is gone, and entries containing an unexpanded variable.

| parameter | type | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `showNoise` | boolean | Include `/usr/bin`, `/bin` and friends, omitted by default as uninformative. |
| `limit` | number | Maximum entries listed. Defaults to 40. |

```
dsh-which · PATH
  9 entries · 8 unique directories
  1 duplicate entry · 1 dead entry

  entries, in resolution order:
    [ 0] C:\Program Files\nodejs
    [ 1] C:\Users\me\AppData\Roaming\npm
    [ 2] C:\Windows\system32
    [ 3] C:\Windows
    [ 4] C:\tools\git\cmd
    [ 5] C:\Program Files\nodejs  — dup of [0]
    [ 6] C:\Users\me\scoop\shims
    [ 7] D:\old-python\Scripts  — missing
    [ 8] C:\Users\me\bin

  Duplicates are usually an installer that prepends itself on every run. Harmless until you edit "the" entry and two copies of it remain.

  Dead entries are skipped silently by every shell, so an uninstalled toolchain leaves a hole that only shows up when its command fails.
```

A dead entry is invisible by construction: shells skip it without a word, so the hole only surfaces later as "command not found" for something that was there yesterday. An unexpanded `%USERPROFILE%` is worse — it can never resolve, no matter what the variable is set to.

### `which_env`

One page describing the command environment: platform, shell, working directory, PATH findings, PATHEXT, and where each common runtime resolves from.

| parameter | type | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `limit` | number | Maximum runtimes listed. Defaults to 30. |

```
dsh-which · environment
  platform: win32  arch x64  node v24.13.0
  shell:    pwsh.exe  (C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe)
  cwd:      C:\repo
  PATH:     9 entries · 8 unique
            1 duplicate · 1 dead
  PATHEXT:  .COM .EXE .BAT .CMD

  resolved runtimes:
    · node  C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.EXE
    · npm  C:\Program Files\nodejs\npm.CMD
    · pnpm  C:\Users\me\AppData\Roaming\npm\pnpm.CMD
    · git  C:\tools\git\cmd\git.EXE
    ✗ python  not found

  1 runtime(s) exist in more than one place on PATH: node
```

The shell line matters more than it looks. `pwsh` and `cmd` disagree about builtins and about `.ps1`, so a report that names the wrong shell is a report nobody should trust.

### `which_sweep`

Sweep a directory of scripts and report, for each name that looks like a command, whether the copy in *that* directory is the one that would run.

| parameter | type | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `directory` | string, **required** | Absolute, or relative to the workspace. |
| `limit` | number | Maximum rows listed. Defaults to 60. |

```
dsh-which · sweep C:\repo\scripts
  3 command(s)
  1 resolve outside this directory (shown with ↪)
  1 do not resolve at all

  ↪ build.cmd  → C:\tools\build\build.cmd
  · deploy.cmd  C:\repo\scripts\deploy.cmd
  ✗ smoke.cmd  does not resolve

  A ↪ means a copy in this directory is not the one that runs: something earlier on PATH wins. That is the usual reason a script behaves differently when called from elsewhere.
```

`./build` and `build` are different programs and nothing warns you. That is the question this answers.

### `which_probe`

Run every copy of a name that resolution can find with a version flag, and report whether they agree.

| parameter | type | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `command` | string, **required** | Command name to probe. |

```
dsh-which · node · version probe
  winner:   v24.13.0
  shadowed: v20.11.1  (C:\Users\me\scoop\shims\node.EXE)

  The copies report different versions. Whatever produced the other version is still installed and still on PATH.
```

Only a known version flag, only files resolution already picked, a four-second timeout, and 8 KB of output per probe. This is not a general command runner.

## Slash command

```
/which              # the environment report
/which node         # what runs
/which node --probe # and what it says its version is
/which --path       # the shape of PATH
/which --env        # the environment report
/which --sweep .    # scripts here that resolve elsewhere
```

## Behaviour

- **Resolution is reimplemented, not shelled out.** The rules live in pure functions over an injected filesystem, so they are tested against fixtures rather than against the machine running the tests.
- **A repeated PATH entry does not double-count a file.** Duplicates are reported by `which_path`; the candidate list answers "how many distinct files carry this name".
- **POSIX skips files that cannot run.** A file with the right name and no executable bit is walked past, and the search continues into later entries — which is what a shell does, and what a listing tool hides.
- **Windows PATHEXT order is honoured.** `.EXE` before `.CMD` means `npm` and `npm.cmd` can be different programs, and an explicit extension is tried before PATHEXT is walked at all.
- **Builtins are not files.** `cd`, `echo`, `dir`, `copy` are answered by the shell; PATH is never consulted.
- **Probing never throws.** A program that hangs, exits non-zero, or does not understand the flag is a result with a reason, not an error. `java -version` exits non-zero and is handled.
- **Nothing is modified.** No PATH editing, no file writes, no environment changes. Reporting is the whole job.
- **The optional workspace service is optional.** Without a workspace registry, relative paths resolve against the process directory; nothing else changes.

## Development

```sh
npm run setup:deps   # link the host's @deepseek-ai/* packages into ./node_modules
npm test             # 88 unit and seam tests
npm run test:live    # 11 checks against the real machine
node test/samples.mjs # regenerate the examples above from the plugin's own renderers
```

The unit tests drive pure modules with a fixture filesystem; the live check runs against the real PATH, the real PATHEXT and a real `node --version`, because that is the one thing fixtures cannot prove. The samples script renders the README examples from a fixed fixture with the plugin's own renderers, so an example cannot drift from the code without the regeneration showing it.

Module layout: `pathlist.js` (PATH itself), `resolve.js` (the rules), `probe.js` (version comparison), `format.js` (rendering), `units.js` (sizes and ages), `host.js` (the only module that touches the real filesystem and environment), `index.js` (tools and command).

      "content": "/**
 * dsh-which — what actually runs when a command is typed.
 *
 * The harness runs commands through a shell, and a shell answers "what does
 * `node` mean" with a rule that is longer than people remember: PATH order,
 * then PATHEXT on Windows or the executable bit elsewhere, with shell builtins
 * short-circuiting the whole thing. Every one of those rules can produce a
 * surprise, and every surprise looks the same from the outside — a command
 * runs, and it is not the one you meant.
 *
 * The failures this exists to name, all of which are silent:
 *
 * - A tool is installed twice, and the older copy is earlier on PATH. The
 *   version you see in your terminal is not the version the agent runs.
 * - An installer prepended itself to PATH on every upgrade, so one directory
 *   now appears three times and editing "the" entry leaves two behind.
 * - An uninstalled toolchain left a dead PATH entry. Shells skip those without
 *   a word, so the hole only surfaces when the command that lived there fails.
 * - A PATH entry contains a literal `%USERPROFILE%` that nothing ever expands,
 *   so it can never resolve.
 * - On Windows, a `.cmd` shim sits in front of a real binary, or a `.ps1`
 *   exists that `cmd` will never run — same name, different behaviour per
 *   shell.
 * - A file exists, has the right name, and is not executable. `ls` shows it;
 *   the shell walks past it to a later PATH entry, or fails.
 *
 * Each of those is a fact about the machine, and none of them is visible from
 * a plain `which`. This plugin reports the resolution *and* what it shadowed,
 * the shape of PATH itself, and — on request — what each copy reports as its
 * version.
 *
 * ## Design commitments
 *
 * 1. **Resolution is reimplemented, not shelled out to `which`.** Shelling out
 *    would inherit the very rules under investigation, and `which` does not
 *    exist on Windows. The rules live in `lib/resolve.js` as pure functions
 *    over an injected filesystem, so they can be tested against fixtures.
 * 2. **Shadowed copies are first-class output.** "What runs" is one line; "what
 *    else answers to this name" is the diagnosis. A report that omits the
 *    shadowed copies cannot explain a version mismatch.
 * 3. **Probing runs only what resolution already chose.** No arbitrary command
 *    execution, only a known version flag, a short timeout, and a bounded
 *    amount of output.
 * 4. **Nothing is changed.** There is no PATH-editing tool here. Reporting is
 *    the whole job; a plugin that silently rewrites PATH is a plugin that
 *    breaks a machine.
 *
 * @module dsh-which
 */

import { join as joinPath, resolve as resolvePath } from 'node:path'

import { defineTool } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools'
import Schema from '@deepseek-ai/schemastery'

import {
  renderEnv,
  renderPath,
  renderProbe,
  renderProblem,
  renderResolve,
  renderSweep,
} from './format.js'
import {
  RUNTIME_CANDIDATES,
  detectShell,
  listDirectory,
  readPath,
  readPathExt,
  statFile,
} from './host.js'
import { analyzePath, foldCase } from './pathlist.js'
import { probeResolution } from './probe.js'
import { isPathCommand, resolveCommand, shadowGroups } from './resolve.js'

/** Plugin name, as the profile's patch file refers to it. */
export const name = 'dsh-which'

/**
 * Services this plugin needs.
 *
 * A static array, not a function: the harness disables a whole bundle whose
 * `inject` is a function, and the failure is silent. Everything else this
 * plugin wants (`workspaceRegistry`) is optional and reached through `ctx.get`.
 */
export const inject = ['tools', 'commands']

/**
 * Per-profile configuration.
 *
 * Every knob that could reasonably differ between machines lives here rather
 * than in a constant, so tuning a profile never means editing code.
 */
export const Config = Schema.object({
  probeTimeoutMs: Schema.number()
    .description('How long a version probe may take before it is abandoned.')
    .default(4000),
  probeByDefault: Schema.boolean()
    .description('Run a version probe on every resolve, without asking. Slower, but the report explains more.')
    .default(false),
  probeShadowedByDefault: Schema.boolean()
    .description('Probe every shadowed copy too, not just the winner. Multiplies the process spawns.')
    .default(false),
  maxSweepFiles: Schema.number()
    .description('Files examined in one sweep of a directory, so a huge directory cannot stall a session.')
    .default(400),
  runtimes: Schema.array(Schema.string())
    .description('Commands the environment report resolves.')
    .default([...RUNTIME_CANDIDATES]),
})

/**
 * Resolve one command against the live machine.
 *
 * @param {string} command - command name or path.
 * @param {{ cwd?: string, env?: Record<string, string | undefined>, platform?: string, pathExt?: string[] }} [options] - environment inputs.
 * @returns {object} the resolution.
 */
export function resolveOnHost(command, options = {}) {
  const env = options.env ?? process.env
  const platform = options.platform ?? process.platform
  const path = readPath(env, { platform })
  const pathExt = options.pathExt ?? readPathExt(env, { platform })

  return resolveCommand(command, {
    entries: path.entries,
    pathExt,
    platform,
    statFile: (candidate) => statFile(qualify(candidate, options.cwd)),
  })
}

/**
 * Make a relative candidate absolute against the working directory.
 *
 * @param {string} candidate - possibly relative path.
 * @param {string} [cwd] - working directory.
 * @returns {string} absolute path.
 */
function qualify(candidate, cwd) {
  if (cwd === undefined) return candidate
  if (/^([a-zA-Z]:[\\/]|[\\/])/u.test(candidate)) return candidate
  return resolvePath(cwd, candidate)
}

/**
 * Analyse the live PATH.
 *
 * @param {{ env?: Record<string, string | undefined>, platform?: string }} [options] - environment inputs.
 * @returns {object} the analysis.
 */
export function analyzeHostPath(options = {}) {
  const env = options.env ?? process.env
  const platform = options.platform ?? process.platform
  const key = Object.keys(env).find((name) => name.toUpperCase() === 'PATH')
  const raw = key === undefined ? '' : env[key] ?? ''
  return analyzePath(raw, { env, platform, exists: (path) => statFile(path) !== undefined })
}

/**
 * Build the environment report.
 *
 * @param {object} config - resolved plugin config.
 * @param {{ cwd?: string, env?: Record<string, string | undefined>, platform?: string }} [options] - environment inputs.
 * @returns {object} the report.
 */
export function buildEnvReport(config, options = {}) {
  const env = options.env ?? process.env
  const platform = options.platform ?? process.platform
  const shell = detectShell(env, { platform })
  const pathAnalysis = analyzeHostPath({ env, platform })

  const runtimes = []
  for (const runtime of config.runtimes ?? []) {
    const resolution = resolveOnHost(runtime, { cwd: options.cwd, env, platform })
    const groups = shadowGroups(resolution)
    runtimes.push({
      name: runtime,
      winner: resolution.winner?.path,
      shadowCount: groups.reduce((total, group) => total + group.entries.length, 0),
    })
  }

  return {
    platform,
    arch: process.arch,
    node: process.version,
    shell: shell.name,
    shellPath: shell.path,
    shellKind: shell.kind,
    cwd: options.cwd ?? process.cwd(),
    path: pathAnalysis,
    ...(platform === 'win32' ? { pathext: readPathExt(env, { platform }) } : {}),
    runtimes,
  }
}

/**
 * Sweep a directory: for each file that looks like a command, where does the
 * name resolve to?
 *
 * The question this answers is the one that comes up whenever a repository
 * ships scripts next to a global install: `./build` and `build` are different
 * programs, and nothing warns you.
 *
 * @param {string} directory - directory to sweep.
 * @param {object} config - resolved plugin config.
 * @param {{ cwd?: string, env?: Record<string, string | undefined>, platform?: string }} [options] - environment inputs.
 * @returns {{ directory: string, rows: object[] }} the sweep.
 */
export function sweepDirectory(directory, config, options = {}) {
  const env = options.env ?? process.env
  const platform = options.platform ?? process.platform
  const absolute = qualify(directory, options.cwd)
  const names = listDirectory(absolute).slice(0, config.maxSweepFiles ?? 400)
  const rows = []

  for (const entry of names) {
    if (entry.startsWith('.')) continue
    const facts = statFile(joinPath(absolute, entry))
    if (facts === undefined || facts.directory) continue
    /* Only files that carry an extension Windows would run, or that are
     * executable elsewhere, look like commands at all. */
    const looksRunnable = platform === 'win32'
      ? /\.(exe|com|cmd|bat|ps1)$/iu.test(entry)
      : facts.executable
    if (!looksRunnable) continue

    const resolution = resolveOnHost(entry, { cwd: options.cwd, env, platform })
    const here = joinPath(absolute, entry)
    const winnerPath = resolution.winner?.path
    /* The sweep answers one question per file: if this directory is on PATH,
     * does its own copy run, or does something earlier win? A row is marked
     * only when the answer is "something earlier" — which is why the test is
     * against this directory, not merely "a winner exists". Comparing folded
     * paths keeps Windows, where case does not distinguish files, honest. */
    const resolvesElsewhere = winnerPath !== undefined
      && foldCase(winnerPath, platform) !== foldCase(here, platform)
    rows.push({
      name: entry,
      winner: winnerPath,
      shadowedBy: resolvesElsewhere ? winnerPath : undefined,
      note: resolution.note,
    })
  }

  return { directory: absolute, rows }
}

/**
 * Run one version probe with the plugin's timeout.
 *
 * @param {object} resolution - a resolution.
 * @param {object} config - resolved plugin config.
 * @param {{ includeShadowed?: boolean, signal?: AbortSignal, platform?: string }} [options] - probe options.
 * @returns {Promise<object>} the probe outcome.
 */
function probeWith(resolution, config, options = {}) {
  return probeResolution(resolution, {
    includeShadowed: options.includeShadowed ?? config.probeShadowedByDefault === true,
    timeoutMs: config.probeTimeoutMs,
    signal: options.signal,
    platform: options.platform,
  })
}

/**
 * Read the session's working directory, when the harness exposes one.
 *
 * Optional service: a deployment without a workspace registry still resolves
 * commands, it just cannot resolve a relative path against the session's root.
 *
 * @param {object} ctx - plugin context.
 * @param {object} exec - tool execution.
 * @returns {string | undefined} the working directory.
 */
function workspaceRootFor(ctx, exec) {
  try {
    const registry = typeof ctx.get === 'function' ? ctx.get('workspaceRegistry') : undefined
    if (registry === undefined) return undefined
    const session = exec?.agent?.session
    if (session !== undefined && typeof registry.forSession === 'function') {
      const root = registry.forSession(session)
      if (typeof root === 'string' && root !== '') return root
    }
    if (typeof registry.current === 'function') {
      const current = registry.current()
      if (typeof current === 'string' && current !== '') return current
    }
    if (typeof registry.defaultRoot === 'function') {
      const root = registry.defaultRoot()
      if (typeof root === 'string' && root !== '') return root
    }
  } catch {
    /* An optional service that throws is the same as one that is absent. */
  }
  return undefined
}

/**
 * Register the tools and the command.
 *
 * @param {object} ctx - plugin context.
 * @param {object} config - resolved config.
 */
export function apply(ctx, config) {
  const cwdFor = (exec) => workspaceRootFor(ctx, exec)

  ctx.tools.register(
    defineTool({
      name: 'which_resolve',
      description:
        'Resolve a command name the way a shell would and report what actually runs: which PATH entry wins, what kind of file it is, and every other copy of the same name that is being shadowed. Use it when a command behaves differently than expected, when a version disagrees between a terminal and the agent, or before telling the user a tool is missing. Pass probe: true to also run each copy with a version flag and compare what they report.',
